title: A Key Turned by Many Hands
paragraphs: The Rosetta Stone is often described as the key that unlocked ancient Egypt, but the metaphor hides a slower and more contested story. Discovered in seventeen ninety nine by French soldiers during Napoleon's Egyptian campaign, the slab was surrendered to Britain after the French defeat and has been displayed in the British Museum since eighteen oh two. It carries a single decree in three scripts, which is why some scholars stress that it is bilingual, not trilingual: Egyptian appears twice, in hieroglyphic and Demotic form, alongside Greek. In that sense, the stone is better understood as a starting point than as a solution.

Because scholars could read the Greek, the stone offered an unprecedented chance to compare texts. Yet a comparison alone proved insufficient, because it was widely assumed that hieroglyphs recorded ideas rather than sounds. The English scientist Thomas Young made a real breakthrough in the early eighteen hundreds by showing that the hieroglyphic and Demotic texts shared striking similarities. It fell to the Frenchman Jean-Francois Champollion, however, to demonstrate that many signs also spelled sounds, a conclusion he announced in eighteen twenty two. Progress depended on patience, on rival theories, and on scholars who were willing to correct one another.

Historians still debate how to divide the credit. Young supplied an early and essential insight, while Champollion's command of languages allowed him to turn that insight into a working system. The episode suggests that decipherment was less a single moment of genius than a chain of partial advances. National pride added further pressure, since both Britain and France wanted the honour of success.
